title: The Giralda has ramps, not stairs
body: The Giralda bell tower was a minaret before it became the Cathedral's tower. Inside there are 35 ramps instead of stairs, wide enough for a man on horseback to ride up for the call to prayer.

title: Columbus is buried in the Cathedral
body: Christopher Columbus's tomb is carried by four statues representing the old kingdoms of Spain. DNA tests in the 2000s supported that the remains are his.

title: What to wear in the Cathedral
body: The Cathedral is a working church: shoulders and knees should be covered, and hats come off. Book ahead to skip the queue; the line can be long late morning.

title: The Alcázar is still a royal palace
body: The upper floors of the Real Alcázar are still used by the Spanish royal family when they visit Seville, which makes it the oldest royal palace in Europe still in use.

title: Alcázar tickets
body: Tickets for the Alcázar sell out at busy times; arriving at opening is the easiest way in. Leave time for the gardens, which take as long as the palace.

title: The tiled province alcoves
body: Around Plaza de España are 48 tiled alcoves, one for each Spanish province, each showing a map and a scene from its history. Spanish visitors often look for their own.

title: Plaza de España in films
body: Plaza de España appeared as the city of Naboo in Star Wars: Attack of the Clones, and in Lawrence of Arabia.

title: Las Setas is made of wood
body: Metropol Parasol, opened in 2011, is often called the largest wooden structure in the world. Roman ruins found while building it are shown in a museum underneath.

title: A market on a castle
body: Triana Market stands on the site of the Castle of San Jorge, seat of the Inquisition in Seville. Its remains can be visited beneath the market.

title: Triana's tiles
body: Triana has made glazed tiles, azulejos, for 500 years. Many tiles in the Alcázar and Plaza de España were made across the river here.

title: Triana and flamenco
body: Triana is one of the cradles of flamenco; many of Seville's best-known singers and dancers came from its old Roma community.

title: Tabs in chalk
body: At El Rinconcillo the waiter chalks your bill on the wooden bar top in front of you. Try the spinach with chickpeas, espinacas con garbanzos.

title: When Seville eats
body: Sevillanos eat lunch around 14:00 to 16:00 and dinner from 21:00. Many kitchens close between 16:30 and 20:00, so tapas bars are the best bet in between.

title: How to order tapas
body: Ordering is done at the bar: ask for una tapa de… and say how many. Standing at the counter is normal and often quicker than a table.

title: Afternoon closing
body: Many small shops close from about 14:00 to 17:30. Big sights and chain stores stay open.

title: The orange trees
body: Seville has around 40,000 bitter orange trees. The oranges are too sour to eat and most are shipped to Britain for marmalade.

title: Murillo's city
body: Bartolomé Esteban Murillo was born in Seville in 1617; the Museum of Fine Arts holds the best collection of his work, in the old convent church.

title: The Archive is free
body: Entry to the Archive of the Indies is free. Its documents include letters from Columbus and Cervantes.

title: Visiting the bullring
body: The Maestranza is visited on a guided tour of the ring, the chapel and the museum; no bullfight needs to be on.

title: Machado's lemon tree
body: The poet Antonio Machado was born at the Palacio de las Dueñas in 1875 and remembered its patio with a lemon tree in his best-known poem.

title: The Alameda at night
body: The Alameda de Hércules fills up after 21:00 with locals on bar terraces. It is the least touristy place in the centre for a drink.

title: Watching flamenco
body: At a small flamenco show, stay quiet during the singing and don't film. Clapping, palmas, is part of the music, so wait to applaud until the dancer finishes.

title: Plaza del Salvador
body: The square in front of El Salvador is where locals meet for a drink at midday and after work, standing outside the small bars.

title: Why the Golden Tower
body: The Torre del Oro may be named after the golden shine of its original tiles reflected in the river, not after gold stored inside.

title: Rain in Seville
body: When it rains in Seville, locals head indoors to markets, churches and tapas bars; outdoor plazas empty quickly and the cobbles get slippery.

title: How the shot tower worked
body: Lead shot for hunting was made here: molten lead was poured through a sieve at the top, and the drops became round as they fell into water at the bottom. Today a camera obscura at the top projects live views of the city onto a table.

title: Why it is called La Carbonería
body: Carbonería means coal shop: the bar fills an old coal yard in Santa Cruz. Flamenco there is informal and free, so arrive early for a seat near the stage.

title: Churros for breakfast
body: In Seville churros are eaten in the morning, dipped in thick hot chocolate. Bar El Comercio is one of the classic places to have them; order at the counter.

title: Miguel de Mañara and the Caridad
body: The hospital was run by the brotherhood of Miguel de Mañara, a nobleman who gave his life to caring for the poor. Its church holds Valdés Leal's paintings of death, In Ictu Oculi and Finis Gloriae Mundi, and works by Murillo.

title: Carmen worked here
body: The Royal Tobacco Factory employed thousands of women rolling cigars. It is the setting of Carmen, the story by Mérimée that Bizet turned into an opera. It is now the main building of the University of Seville, and you can walk in on weekdays.

title: Roman floors in a Seville house
body: The Countess of Lebrija paved her house with Roman mosaics brought from the ruins of Itálica, just outside Seville. The ground floor around the patio is the reason to visit.

title: The square of the doves
body: Plaza de América is known locally for its white doves, which gather between the pavilions built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition. Two of the pavilions house the Archaeological Museum and the Museum of Popular Arts and Customs.

title: The Inquisition in Triana
body: The castle of San Jorge was the seat of the Spanish Inquisition in Seville. Its foundations survive under Triana Market, and the small museum explains what happened there.

title: Monastery, then ceramics factory
body: Columbus stayed at the Cartuja monastery while preparing his voyages. In the 19th century it became the Pickman ceramics factory, and its tall brick kilns still stand among the contemporary art.

title: The Esperanza de Triana
body: This chapel is home to the Esperanza de Triana, one of the most loved images of Seville's Holy Week. Triana's sailors and potters have kept it for centuries, and locals drop in daily to see her.

title: The Lord of Seville
body: Jesús del Gran Poder, carved by Juan de Mesa in the 17th century, is so revered that locals call him the Lord of Seville. The basilica is free and quiet outside mass times.

title: A fish market by the river
body: The iron-and-glass hall was built in the 19th century as the city fish market, beside the Triana bridge. Today its stalls serve tapas and drinks from morning until late, a covered option when it rains.
